Then he looks up at the doorframe, at the stack of chalk bands, the green paint, the violet year, and sees that there is no color left in his pocket that nobody has used.

So he crushes nothing and chalks nothing. He wets his thumb in the water standing on the step and presses it flat to the bare wood above Orla's violet, and the print darkens, holds for the length of a breath, and begins to fade at its edges as the grain drinks it. He watches it go. When it is gone he does it again, a hand's width higher, and then again, until a row of damp thumbprints climbs the doorframe toward the brass, each one fading as he reaches for the next, and the whole line is visible for only as long as it takes him to finish it.

Down the slope, a door that has stood open all night swings a little wider, and Teodor, who has never heard of a "1" or a "2," goes in to see who left it that way.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
Inside, the house is empty in the ordinary way: a table, two chairs, a cold hearth, a pair of boots by the wall with the heels worn down on the wrong side for walking uphill. Teodor does not know that this matters. He picks one up, finds it too big, and puts it back exactly as he found it, which is the only rule he has.

On the table sits a plate, and on the plate a single honey-cake, old enough to have gone hard and pale, with a thumbprint pressed into the top. He does not eat it. He sets his own wet thumb beside the old one, and the two prints are nearly the same size, which could mean anything or nothing, and he decides not to wonder which.

When he steps back out, the draft has turned. It comes down the slope now, from the Kerrow side toward the water, and every door in Verrel leans with it, slowly, a hand's width closer to shut. Teodor stands in the doorway with the cake in his hand, barefoot, facing the waterline, and waits to see whether anyone will come to knock.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
Nobody knocks. The water stands a finger below the sill, perfectly still for the first time since the thaw, and in it Teodor sees the doorframe reflected, upside down, the stack of bands running down into the dark like a ladder someone has already climbed.

He sets the honey-cake on the step. Not as payment, because there is no one left to pay, but because it seems the right height for it, level with the water, where a thing left out will be either taken or not. Then he sits beside it and puts his feet in.

The cold is exact. It comes up to his ankles and stops there, at a line he could mark if he had chalk, and he finds he does not want to. Somewhere up the slope a door finishes closing, softly, the first one in a hundred years to latch on its own, and Teodor listens to the small click travel down the street, door to door, each one answering the last, until the sound reaches the step and the water carries it out across the reservoir floor.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The click does not come back. Teodor waits for an echo, because the reservoir wall is close enough to give one, and none arrives, which he takes to mean that the sound has gone somewhere the town has not measured yet.

The honey-cake sits level with the water. After a while a ripple reaches it, not from the doors or from his feet, but from out in the middle of the reservoir, where the surface has begun to move in slow, widening rings, as if something below had set down a stone.

He does not count the rings. He leaves his feet where they are, and the rings come on toward the step, one after another, each a little fainter than the last, until the nearest touches the cake's edge and the cold line at his ankles rises, very slightly, by the width of a thumbprint.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The rise holds. Teodor feels it settle against his skin like a hand laid there and left, and he understands, without having words for it, that something has just been written that he will not be asked to read.

Out on the water the rings stop. Where the middle of the reservoir was moving there is only the flat grey surface and the reflected sky, and in the stillness he notices the first thing in all his seven years that he would call a sound meant for him: a single low knock, from far down, wood on wood, patient and unhurried, the way a person knocks who has come a long way and is not sure the door is still a door.

He looks up the slope at the latched doors, and at the one still open behind him, and at the honey-cake, which has begun, very slightly, to float. Then he does what nobody in Verrel has done since the founders: he stands up, wipes his wet feet on the sill, and answers the knock by leaving the door ajar, a hand's width, behind him as he walks down into the water.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The water takes him to the ankles, then the knees, and it is not cold the way the groove was cold. It is the temperature of a room someone has just left, and Teodor, who has never been told what the founders felt on the night the well ran dry, recognizes it anyway.

The knocking comes again, closer now, and he sees what is making it: a door, floating on its back across the reservoir, the Kerrow door with its polished handle, lighter than any door should be, rocking against a drowned fencepost in the swell. Someone has brought it out here to be found by water. The lower edge is still ticked with chalk, and as it turns in the current he sees that the ticks have been joined by a new one, fresh and pale, cut in a hand that leans neither way.

He puts his palm flat on the wood, as Odile did on the rust and Tamsin on the stone. The door does not open. It does not need to. It holds against his hand, patient and unlatched, with the whole town's open doorways behind him facing it, and Teodor understands that this was the thing the founders were waiting for: not the water, but a door on the other side of it, left ajar for them.

He knocks once, to say he has come.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
From somewhere behind the door, or beneath it, or in the draft that has followed him down the slope, comes one knock in answer, so soft that he almost takes it for the pulse in his own palm.

Teodor waits. The door rocks once against the fencepost and settles. Along its lower edge the pale new tick is still wet, and beside it, so close it might be its shadow, the water has begun to pool in a second cut he did not see before, small and slanted, lying the old way.

He does not turn it over. He leaves his hand where it is, and the knock comes a second time, and this time he knocks back before he has decided to.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The two knocks settle into a rhythm, his and the door's, so even that Teodor can no longer tell which one answers which. Out across the reservoir the rings begin again, this time from the far wall, and the water at his knees rises a thumbprint, then another, as though the whole basin were breathing out.

He thinks of the boots with the wrong-sided heels, the hard honey-cake, the click traveling door to door. None of it needs to be explained. He keeps his palm on the wood and the knocking goes on, and behind him, up the slope, the latched doors one by one begin to swing open again, each a hand's width, waiting for whoever comes back up.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
Teodor's hand stays on the wood until the knocking slows, and then it does not stop so much as become something he is carrying. He turns toward the slope with the rhythm still in his wrist.

The water lets him go as gently as it took him. At the step the honey-cake has floated a hand's width from where he left it, and he leaves it there, since it is neither taken nor refused, only moved.

Above him, on the dry shelf of the oldest house, someone has set the two books side by side with their covers open to the same blank line, and the draft turns both pages together.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The pages settle, and the draft, having nothing left to turn, drops to a breath. Teodor climbs the slope past the open doors. At the Marrant step he stops, because the doorframe now carries his row of thumbprints again, dry this time, each one a faint pale ghost in the grain where the damp has gone and the wood remembers.

He does not trace them. He sets his hand against the frame beside them, at the height of his own shoulder, and leaves it there for the length of a held breath.

When he lifts it, the print is already fading, and below on the step the water goes on rising toward the brass, a finger a year, patient, with a door floating out on it somewhere, waiting to be answered by whoever comes next.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
Up the slope, the first door to latch itself swings open again, a hand's width, and holds.

Teodor takes his hand from the frame and goes in to find the boots, because it has occurred to him that someone should wear them down the other way.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
He carries them out into the morning and sits on the step to try them. They are far too big, and he stuffs the toes with a fistful of dry reeds from the second gate, which still grow thick along the foot of the wall, then laces them tight and stands.

The first stride down the slope is clumsy, but the heels bite the mud on the correct side, the one that wears toward the water. By the third street he has stopped noticing the weight. At the lowest sill he leaves a single clean print in the soft ground, and the water slides in to fill it, and he walks on without looking back to see how long it lasts.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The print holds for a moment, bright and rimmed with silt, and then the water finishes it, smoothing the heel to the same grey as everything around it.

Teodor keeps walking along the lowest street, where the doorsteps are all wet now and the old brass marks lie green beneath the surface like coins in a well. At the end of the street he reaches the spillway gate, the first one, rusted shut for as long as anyone has said, and sets his palm on it as he has seen the others do.

It is warm. Not much, but in a town where everything has been cold and damp for a century, the warmth is a plain fact against his hand, and he has no ruler for it. He stands there in the too-big boots, with reeds poking out at the toes, and feels it through his palm: something on the other side of the gate has been recently, patiently, kept.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
Teodor presses his ear to the iron. Behind the rust there is a faint, even sound, not water and not wind, more like a slow breathing, or a pencil being drawn along a ruled line by someone who is in no hurry to finish.

He does not knock. He has already knocked once today, and he has learned from the Kerrow door that an answer is not owed twice. Instead he sits down with his back against the gate, boots stretched out in front of him, and takes the dry reeds from his pockets, the spare ones, and begins to braid them into a small loose cord, for no reason except that his hands want something to do while he listens.

By the time the cord is a hand long, the warmth has spread through the iron into his spine, and the sound behind the gate has changed. It is no longer a line being drawn. It is a pause, the kind a writer leaves when she has reached the end of a row and is waiting to see whether anyone will rule the next.

Teodor ties off the cord, loops it once around the rusted handle, and leaves it there, loosely knotted, so that whoever comes next can untie it without cutting.

Then he gets up and goes back toward the slope, leaving the gate to its keeping.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
Behind him the cord settles against the iron, and the warmth in the gate does not fade as he walks away. It holds, patient as the draft.

At the foot of the slope he passes the Marrant step and the two books lying open to the same blank line. He does not stop. The water has risen another thumbprint against the sill, and the doors above him stand a hand's width ajar, waiting.

He climbs in the too-big boots, heels biting the mud on the side that wears toward the water, and at the top, in the empty Kerrow frame, he stands where the door once hung and looks back down the whole slope of the town. From here every open doorway lines up with the next, down to the reservoir, and he sees, small at the lowest end, the first gate with a pale cord looped through its handle.

A single door below him swings once and stays.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
From the empty Kerrow frame, Teodor can see something he could not see from the step: the lowest street runs straight to the gate, and the open doors on either side lean toward it, forty-one and two, so the whole town forms a long, shallow funnel with the cord at its narrow end.

He thinks of the first sentence anyone told him, which was nobody's, just the habit of the place: put it back the way you found it. Standing here, he sees that the town has done exactly that. Everything it kept dry, it kept dry so that someone could come and find it as it was.

He leaves his hand on the frame where the hinges were, still bright with oil. Then he sits on the threshold, boots dangling over the drop to the barn, and watches the light move down the slope, door by door, until it reaches the water and goes in.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The light does not come back out. Teodor waits for a glint, a flash off the surface, and the water takes it the way the sealed folds once took the children's guesses: quietly, with no sign of what it has been told.

Behind him, in the barn, something shifts on the trestles. He does not turn. The empty hinges at his shoulder have begun to cool, and he understands that the oil was never meant to keep a door swinging but to keep a place ready, so that anyone who came back would find the metal free.

He takes one of the reeds still in his pocket, the last, and lays it across the lowest hinge pin, loosely, the way he laid the cord on the gate. Then he stays where he is, on the threshold, with the town spread below him and every doorway open to the same slow draft, and a new sentence arrives in his head that nobody gave him. He does not say it aloud, because it is only a sentence, and the slope is listening.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The sentence stays unspoken, and the slope goes on listening. Teodor sits until the light has gone off the last brass mark and the first stars come down into the reservoir, one by one, each taken without a sound.

When his legs grow stiff he gets up, leaves the reed across the hinge pin, and walks back down the slope in the dark. Every door he passes is open its hand's width, and from each comes the same faint smell of wet iron. At the Marrant step the two books are still there. He does not read them. He lies down beside them with the too-big boots still on, and the water lays its cold line across his ankles, just under the laces.

Before he sleeps, he says the sentence, very quietly, to the water instead of the slope, because the water has never asked anyone to prove anything. What he says is not recorded. In the morning a seven-year-old will find a boy-shaped dry place on the step, two books touching, and a pair of boots left neatly at the sill with reeds in the toes, heels worn the right way. She will put them back as she found them.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The seven-year-old is named Isolde, and she finds the boots as the rule says, then spends a long moment with her hand hovering over them, because the rule says to put things back and does not say where the boy has gone.

She looks down the street. The footprints have already been smoothed by the water, but at the lowest step there is a faint wet trail leading not toward the gate or the slope but out onto the reservoir floor, where the shallow water lies thin over cracked mud, and far out, small and dark against the flat grey, a figure is walking with the unhurried gait of someone who has been answered.

She does not call after him. She sets the boots on the step, heels toward the water, and tucks a dry reed into each toe, because it seems the right thing to leave in them. Then she takes the rag from her pocket, and since there is no brass to polish and no color left and no one to pay her, she dips it in the water and wipes the doorframe once, from the bottom band to the top, until the whole stack of chalk lines runs together into a single soft stripe, every color at once, no hand in it.

When it dries it will read as nothing in particular. She steps back, and the draft comes down the slope and lifts a corner of the nearest book, and she lets it turn.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The page turns once and lies still. Isolde watches the figure shrink until the grey takes it, and finds she does not need to see where it stops.

She sits down on the step beside the boots, puts her feet in the water, and waits for whatever the draft brings next.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The draft brings nothing at first, and she lets it. The water at her ankles is cold and exact, and the soft stripe on the doorframe is already drying paler at the edges, where the colors have begun to separate again as the damp leaves them.

Then, from the lowest street, a small sound: a rag being wrung out. A girl she has never seen, perhaps six, stands at the corner with a rag of her own and a look of someone rehearsing being hired. She does not ask what the stripe is for. She looks at it, then at Isolde's feet in the water, then at the boots with their reeds, and says that she turns seven in the spring and wants to know if there is anything she should do before then.

Isolde thinks about it for the length of a held breath. Then she says that there is one rule, and that she can tell it, since the rule is only a habit and has never belonged to anyone: put it back the way you found it, and then look at what you've found.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The girl nods slowly, the way someone nods who has been given a thing too large to hold yet and is deciding where to set it down. She wrings her rag out once more, though it is already dry, and sits on the step a hand's width from Isolde, close enough to share the cold but not close enough to be counted as company.

"What do I look at first?" she asks.

Isolde does not answer. She points down the street, past the boots and the stripe, to where the water lies flat over the lowest step. The girl follows her finger and looks, and neither of them says what is there. A ripple comes in from the far reservoir, faint and widening, and reaches the step, and the cold line at their ankles rises by a thumbprint.

The girl puts her rag in the water and holds it there. Behind them the draft turns another page, and no one reads it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The rag darkens in the girl's hand and grows heavy, and she lets it hang there without wringing it, as though the water were a thing that should be allowed to finish.

Isolde watches the ripple's edge move on past the step and up the slope, wetting the first dry stone it reaches. She does not follow it. She has noticed that the six-year-old's feet do not yet touch the water, only the rag does, and that this is a correct place to begin: one hand's width removed, with something between herself and the cold.

"It's lower than I thought," the girl says at last, meaning the water, or the step, or her own place on it. Isolde nods. Behind them, in the oldest house, a door that has been ajar for a century finishes opening, quietly, all the way.
